title: Heuristic Evaluation — What It Is and What It Is Not
content:
A heuristic evaluation is a structured expert inspection of an interface against a defined set of usability principles. It produces a prioritised list of specific, located, severity-rated problems with recommended fixes.

WHAT IT IS GOOD AT: finding the obvious problems cheaply, before you spend money on users. Fast (hours, not weeks), needs no recruitment, works on competitor products and on unbuilt designs, and produces a shared vocabulary a team can argue in.

WHAT IT IS NOT: a substitute for usability testing. It tells you what violates a principle; it does not tell you what real people will do. Experts predict roughly the right problems and consistently miss the ones that come from real context — unfamiliarity, distraction, domain ignorance, and motivation. Run heuristic evaluation FIRST to clear the obvious defects, then test with users on what remains.

THE EVALUATOR-COUNT FINDING (Nielsen & Molich, 1990): a single evaluator finds roughly 35% of the problems present. Three to five evaluators working independently find the large majority. Beyond five, returns fall off sharply. Independence is the whole mechanism — evaluators who discuss findings before finishing converge on the same subset and the coverage gain disappears.

THE MOST COMMON FAILURE: treating it as a checklist to pass. A heuristic violation is a hypothesis about a problem, weighted by severity and context. Some violations are correct decisions. 'Aesthetic and minimalist design' and 'flexibility and efficiency of use' pull in opposite directions constantly; the evaluation surfaces the tension, it does not resolve it.

title: Nielsen 1 — Visibility of System Status
content:
PRINCIPLE: the system should always keep users informed about what is going on, through appropriate feedback within reasonable time.

HOW IT FAILS IN PRACTICE:
- An action with no acknowledgement. Tapping 'Save' and nothing changes, so the user taps again.
- Loading with no indication of progress or duration. A spinner past ~3 seconds stops reassuring and starts worrying.
- No indication of WHERE you are — no active nav state, no breadcrumb, no step count in a multi-step flow.
- Background processes invisible. An upload continuing, a sync running, a draft autosaving with no trace.
- Optimistic UI that lies. Showing success before the server confirms, then silently reverting.

HOW TO CHECK: perform every action on the screen and ask, for each, 'how do I know it worked?' Then ask 'how do I know it is still working?' and 'how do I know where I am?'

DOMAIN SPECIFICS:
- Shopify: add-to-cart with no visible confirmation is a measurable conversion loss. The cart count, the drawer, or an inline confirmation must fire immediately.
- Crypto: this heuristic is the whole product. Pending / confirming / confirmed / failed must each be a distinct, named, visible state with an explanation of elapsed and expected time. A transaction in an unknown state is the defining trust failure of the category.
- AI: the user needs to know the model is working, what it is working ON (which documents, which context), and roughly how long. A bare spinner during a 20-second generation is a status failure, not a loading state.

SEVERITY TENDENCY: high. Status failures cause duplicate actions, abandonment, and support tickets.

title: Nielsen 2 — Match Between System and the Real World
content:
PRINCIPLE: speak the users' language, with words, phrases and concepts familiar to them, rather than system-oriented terms. Follow real-world conventions, making information appear in a natural and logical order.

HOW IT FAILS:
- Internal vocabulary leaking out. 'Entity', 'record', 'object', 'instance', 'payload', 'sync token'.
- Domain jargon assumed rather than taught. 'Gas', 'slippage', 'nonce', 'seed phrase', 'metafield', 'variant', 'embedding', 'context window'.
- Ordering that follows the database, not the task. A form that asks for the least important thing first because that is the table's first column.
- Icons with no real-world referent. A floppy disk for save is now archaeology; an abstract glyph invented for your product is worse.
- Units and formats that require conversion. Cents instead of currency, epoch timestamps, hex colour codes shown to a shopper.

HOW TO CHECK: read every label out loud as if speaking to the actual user. Any word you would not say in that conversation is a violation. Then check the order of information against how the user thinks about the task, not how the system stores it.

THE NUANCE FOR CRYPTO AND AI: some jargon is load-bearing and cannot be removed without removing precision — 'gas' has no plain-English equivalent that is also accurate. The correct move is not to hide the term but to teach it in place: the term, plus what it means for this user, plus what it costs them, at the moment they need it. Renaming 'gas' to 'network fee' is usually right; renaming 'seed phrase' to something friendlier is dangerous, because the user needs to recognise the real term when a scammer uses it.

SEVERITY TENDENCY: medium to high, and higher for new users.

title: Nielsen 3 — User Control and Freedom
content:
PRINCIPLE: users often choose system functions by mistake and need a clearly marked emergency exit. Support undo and redo.

HOW IT FAILS:
- No undo on a destructive action. A confirmation dialog is a WEAKER pattern than undo, because it interrupts everyone to protect the rare mistake. Prefer undo; use confirmation only when undo is genuinely impossible.
- Modals with no visible close. Or close-on-outside-click disabled on something abandonable.
- Flows with no exit. A five-step wizard that traps the user with no 'save and finish later' and no back.
- Irreversible defaults. A destructive action as the primary, styled button.
- Losing work on navigation. Back button clearing a filled form.
- Autoplay, auto-advance, or auto-redirect with no stop.

HOW TO CHECK: for every action, ask 'can I take this back?' For every screen, ask 'can I leave?' For every flow, ask 'can I pause?'

THE HARD CASE — GENUINELY IRREVERSIBLE ACTIONS: crypto transactions, real payments, published content, sent messages, deleted accounts. Here you cannot offer undo, so you owe the user:
1. A confirmation that restates the specific consequence in the user's terms, not a generic 'Are you sure?'.
2. Friction proportional to the stakes — type-to-confirm for account deletion, a review screen for a transaction.
3. No default-focused destructive button, no dismiss-by-outside-click.
4. A delay window where possible. Even 5 seconds of 'Undo' on a sent message prevents most regret.

SEVERITY TENDENCY: high, and severity 4 when the action is irreversible and involves money or data loss.

title: Nielsen 4 — Consistency and Standards
content:
PRINCIPLE: users should not have to wonder whether different words, situations, or actions mean the same thing. Follow platform and industry conventions.

TWO KINDS, BOTH REQUIRED:
- INTERNAL consistency — the same thing looks and behaves the same way everywhere in your product. Violations: three button styles for the same priority, two different date formats, 'Delete' in one place and 'Remove' in another for the same operation, a modal that closes on outside-click on one screen and not another.
- EXTERNAL consistency (Jakob's Law) — you match the conventions users have learned elsewhere. Violations: a non-standard checkout flow, a logo that does not link home, a search icon that does something else, a cart in an unexpected place, a swipe gesture that means the opposite of the platform default.

HOW TO CHECK: build an inventory. Screenshot every button, every input, every empty state, every error message across the product and put them side by side. Inconsistency is invisible screen by screen and glaring in a grid. This is also the fastest design-debt audit that exists.

WHEN TO BREAK CONVENTION: only when you have evidence the convention is worse for your specific users, and only in one place at a time. Novelty spends the user's attention; you get a small budget and it should go to the thing that differentiates you, not to your date picker.

DESIGN SYSTEM CONNECTION: most consistency violations are governance failures, not design failures. If three button styles exist, the question is not 'which is right' but 'why did the system permit three'. Fix the component, not the screen.

SEVERITY TENDENCY: individually low (often cosmetic), collectively high — inconsistency is how a product comes to feel untrustworthy without any single identifiable defect.

title: Nielsen 5 — Error Prevention
content:
PRINCIPLE: better than good error messages is a careful design which prevents a problem from occurring in the first place.

THE TWO ERROR TYPES (Norman) AND THEIR DIFFERENT CURES:
- SLIPS — the user intended the right thing and did the wrong thing. Cure with constraints, larger targets, spacing between dangerous and safe actions, and undo. Fitts's Law is an error-prevention tool: a destructive button adjacent to a common one guarantees slips.
- MISTAKES — the user intended the wrong thing because their model of the system was wrong. Cure with better information, clearer labels, defaults that encode the right choice, and inline explanation at the point of decision.

PREVENTION TECHNIQUES, IN ORDER OF STRENGTH:
1. Make the error impossible. Disable unavailable options. Do not offer an out-of-stock size as selectable. Constrain the input type.
2. Encode the right answer as the default. Most users accept defaults; a good default prevents more errors than any message.
3. Validate as the user goes, not on submit. Inline, adjacent to the field, on blur rather than on keystroke.
4. Confirm only the genuinely irreversible.
5. Show the consequence before the commitment. Gas estimate before signing, total including shipping before checkout, what the AI will change before it changes it.

HOW TO CHECK: for every input, ask 'what is the most likely wrong thing here, and what stops it?' For every destructive control, ask 'what is adjacent to it?'

SHOPIFY SPECIFIC: the highest-value prevention is inventory and variant logic — never let a user select a combination that cannot be purchased, and show shipping cost before the checkout step where surprise cost causes abandonment.

SEVERITY TENDENCY: high. Prevented errors never generate support load.

title: Nielsen 6 — Recognition Rather Than Recall
content:
PRINCIPLE: minimise the user's memory load by making objects, actions, and options visible. Users should not have to remember information from one part of the interface to another.

HOW IT FAILS:
- Information needed on step 3 that was only shown on step 1. An order summary absent from the payment screen. A verification code the user must memorise from another screen.
- Hidden functionality. Actions available only on hover, only via right-click, only via an unhinted gesture, only via a command palette with no discoverable entry.
- Icon-only controls with no label and no tooltip. A row of six ambiguous glyphs is a memory test.
- Requiring the user to remember what they typed. A search results page that does not show the query. A filtered list that does not show the active filters.
- Codes and identifiers the user must transcribe rather than select or copy.

HOW TO CHECK: walk the flow and note every moment you need information that is not currently on screen. Then hide the interface and ask what the user would have to remember to continue.

MILLER'S LAW CONNECTION: working memory holds roughly four chunks reliably, not seven. Any design requiring the user to hold more than a few items across a transition is asking for failure.

AI SPECIFIC: this heuristic is where most AI interfaces fail. A bare text box requires the user to RECALL what the system can do. Showing capabilities contextually — example prompts, visible tools, surfaced actions relevant to the current selection — converts recall into recognition and is the single highest-leverage change to most AI UIs.

CRYPTO SPECIFIC: never require a user to compare a wallet address by memory. Show both, truncate identically, and highlight the matching characters.

SEVERITY TENDENCY: medium to high; usually shows up as slowness and error rate rather than outright failure.

title: Nielsen 7 — Flexibility and Efficiency of Use
content:
PRINCIPLE: accelerators — unseen by the novice — may often speed up interaction for the expert, such that the system can cater to both inexperienced and experienced users. Allow users to tailor frequent actions.

HOW IT FAILS:
- No path for expertise. Every user, every time, walks the same guided flow. A power user doing this fifty times a day is being taxed by an onboarding pattern.
- Onboarding that cannot be skipped, or that reappears.
- No keyboard support. No shortcuts, no tab order, no Enter to submit, no Escape to close.
- No bulk operations where the task is inherently plural.
- No saved state — no recent items, no saved searches, no saved filters, no templates, no defaults learned from behaviour.
- Accelerators that are the ONLY path, which fails the novice instead.

HOW TO CHECK: do the primary task once as a first-timer, then imagine doing it for the fiftieth time. Count the steps. If the count is identical, the interface has no flexibility. Then check the keyboard: can you complete the primary task without a mouse?

THE TENSION WITH HEURISTIC 8: accelerators add interface. The resolution is progressive disclosure — the accelerator exists but does not occupy visual weight. Keyboard shortcuts shown in tooltips. Bulk selection appearing only on first selection. A command palette behind one discoverable key.

AI SPECIFIC: the novice needs a guided, suggested-prompt interface; the expert needs raw access, system-prompt control, and repeatable templates. Supporting only one of the two is the most common shape of AI product failure — either it is a toy or it is a blank box.

SEVERITY TENDENCY: low for consumer, high for professional tools. In a tool used daily, this heuristic is a retention issue.

title: Nielsen 8 — Aesthetic and Minimalist Design
content:
PRINCIPLE: dialogues should not contain information which is irrelevant or rarely needed. Every extra unit of information competes with the relevant units and diminishes their relative visibility.

NOTE THE ACTUAL CLAIM. This is not 'make it look nice' and not 'use less content'. It is a claim about COMPETITION for attention. The test is relative visibility, not absolute quantity. A dense trading interface can pass; a sparse marketing page with three competing CTAs can fail.

HOW IT FAILS:
- Multiple primary CTAs at the same visual weight. The user must decide what the product wants, which is the product's job.
- Every element emphasised. Six badges, four colours of text, three levels of bold on one card. When everything is loud, nothing is.
- Explanatory copy nobody asked for. Helper text under a field whose label is already clear.
- Decorative imagery occupying the position of the primary action.
- Notification and banner accretion — a cookie notice, a promo bar, an app-install prompt, and a newsletter modal stacking above the content.
- Data with no hierarchy. A table where every column has equal weight.

HOW TO CHECK: squint, or blur the screen. What remains legible should be exactly the priority order you intended. Then count the things asking for attention; if it is more than three, cut. Then remove elements one at a time and ask what breaks — anything that breaks nothing was competing for nothing.

THE TENSION: this heuristic pulls against 1 (status), 6 (recognition), 7 (flexibility) and 10 (help), all of which add interface. Minimalism that removes status feedback or hides functionality is a worse outcome, and 'clean' is the most common justification for interfaces that hide what users need. Resolve with hierarchy, not deletion.

SEVERITY TENDENCY: usually 2–3; higher when it obscures the primary action or a conversion path.

title: Nielsen 9 — Help Users Recognise, Diagnose, and Recover From Errors
content:
PRINCIPLE: error messages should be expressed in plain language (no codes), precisely indicate the problem, and constructively suggest a solution.

THE THREE-PART TEST — every error message must answer:
1. WHAT happened, in plain language.
2. WHY, specifically enough to be actionable.
3. WHAT TO DO NEXT, as a concrete action, ideally as a button.

HOW IT FAILS:
- Generic messages. 'Something went wrong.' 'Invalid input.' 'Error 500.' These fail all three parts.
- Error codes with no translation. Acceptable only as a secondary detail for support, never as the message.
- Messages far from the cause. A summary at the top of a long form telling the user 'there were errors' without saying where.
- Blame. 'You entered an invalid email.' The system's failures in particular must own themselves — 'We could not reach the server' not 'Your request failed'.
- Errors that destroy work. A validation failure that clears the fields.
- No recovery path. A dead end with no retry, no back, no support link.
- Errors as the only feedback channel — a red border with no text fails screen reader users entirely.

HOW TO CHECK: trigger every error you can. Submit empty, submit malformed, disconnect the network, revoke the permission, exhaust the balance. Read each message against the three-part test.

DOMAIN SPECIFICS:
- Crypto: 'Transaction failed' is unacceptable. Say whether funds moved, whether gas was consumed, and what to do — this is the difference between a bad moment and a lost user.
- AI: distinguish 'I cannot do that' (capability), 'I will not do that' (policy), 'I do not have enough information' (input), and 'something broke' (system). Collapsing these into one message destroys the user's ability to adapt.

SEVERITY TENDENCY: high. Errors are where users are already frustrated, so the cost of a bad message compounds.

title: Nielsen 10 — Help and Documentation
content:
PRINCIPLE: it is better if the system can be used without documentation, but it may be necessary to provide help. Any such information should be easy to search, focused on the user's task, list concrete steps, and not be too large.

HOW IT FAILS:
- Help that is a separate destination requiring the user to leave the task, then find their way back and re-establish context.
- Documentation organised by the product's structure rather than the user's questions.
- A tutorial shown once, at the moment of least motivation, and never available again.
- Tooltips as the only explanation for something that needs real explanation — and inaccessible on touch.
- No help at the moment of decision. The user needs to know what 'slippage tolerance' means while setting it, not in an FAQ.
- Help that explains the interface rather than the task. 'Click the button to submit' teaches nothing.

HOW TO CHECK: at every decision point in the flow, ask 'what would a reasonable person not know here, and where do they find out?' Then check whether finding out costs them their place.

WHAT GOOD LOOKS LIKE:
- Contextual, in-place, dismissible. A short explanation adjacent to the control it explains.
- Progressive. One line inline, expandable to a paragraph, linking to the full document.
- Task-shaped headings. 'How do I get a refund' beats 'Refund policy'.
- Re-accessible. Anything shown in onboarding must be findable afterwards.

AI SPECIFIC: the interface should teach prompting through use — example prompts, visible capability hints, feedback on why something did not work. An AI product whose help is a documentation site has offloaded its hardest design problem.

SEVERITY TENDENCY: usually 1–2 in consumer products, higher in complex domains where the cost of not knowing is money (crypto, B2B tooling).

title: Severity Ratings — Making Findings Actionable
content:
Nielsen's 0–4 scale:
- 0 — not a usability problem at all. Use it; disagreeing evaluators need somewhere to land.
- 1 — COSMETIC. Fix only if extra time is available.
- 2 — MINOR usability problem. Low priority.
- 3 — MAJOR usability problem. Important to fix, high priority.
- 4 — USABILITY CATASTROPHE. Imperative to fix before release.

RATE ON THREE FACTORS, COMBINED:
- FREQUENCY — how many users hit it, how often. A problem on the checkout button affects everyone; a problem in account settings affects a fraction.
- IMPACT — how hard is it to overcome when hit. Confusing versus blocking.
- PERSISTENCE — is it a one-time learning cost or a repeated tax? A confusing label learned once is cheaper than a mis-sized target that fails 5% of the time forever.

A high score on any one factor can justify a 3; high on all three is a 4.

HOW TO USE THE RATINGS WELL:
- Rate independently, then compare. Divergence in ratings is information — it usually means evaluators disagree about frequency, which is an empirical question you can answer with analytics rather than argument.
- Average across evaluators rather than debating to consensus. Nielsen's guidance is that averaged ratings are more reliable than negotiated ones.
- Attach a business consequence where you can. '4 — blocks purchase on mobile Safari, which is 61% of sessions' moves faster through a backlog than '4 — catastrophe'.
- Do not inflate. A team that receives thirty severity-4 findings stops reading severity ratings.

WHAT SEVERITY IS NOT: a measure of how much the finding annoys you, or how easy it is to fix. Effort is a separate axis, and combining severity with effort is what produces a prioritised plan — high severity / low effort first.
source: NN/g — Severity Ratings for Usability Problems

title: Running a Heuristic Evaluation — Full Protocol
content:
PREPARE
1. Define scope narrowly: one flow, one device, one user group, one goal. 'The whole app' produces a shallow evaluation.
2. Write the user tasks you will walk. Real tasks, in the user's words.
3. Choose the heuristic set. Nielsen's 10 as the base; add domain heuristics (see he-015, he-016) where relevant.
4. Recruit 3–5 evaluators. Double-experts (usability plus domain knowledge) find substantially more than usability generalists.
5. Set up the capture format before starting — one row per finding, with the required fields (he-014).

EVALUATE (1–2 hours per evaluator, independently)
6. First pass: walk the flow freely, getting a feel for it. Note nothing.
7. Second pass: walk each defined task deliberately, inspecting each screen against each heuristic.
8. Third pass: walk as an experienced user, looking for efficiency and flexibility failures.
9. Inspect the states, not just the happy path — empty, loading, error, overflow, disabled.
10. Record every finding with its location, screenshot, heuristic, and severity. Do not filter while evaluating.
11. DO NOT DISCUSS with other evaluators until everyone has finished. This is the mechanism, not a formality.

CONSOLIDATE
12. Merge duplicates, keeping the clearest description.
13. Affinity-map by area or theme.
14. Average the severity ratings rather than negotiating them.
15. Cut findings that are preference, not principle. If you cannot name the heuristic, it is an opinion — still possibly valid, but label it as such.
16. Prioritise on severity × effort and identify what needs user testing to resolve.

TIME BUDGET: 1–2 hours evaluating per person, 2 hours consolidating, 1 hour writing up. A five-person evaluation is roughly two person-days total for a substantially complete problem list.
source: NN/g — How to Conduct a Heuristic Evaluation

title: Finding Format — How to Write a Usability Finding
content:
Every finding needs these fields. Anything missing makes it un-actionable.

- ID — sequential, so it can be referenced in a backlog.
- LOCATION — screen, component, and state. 'Checkout, step 2, payment method, error state'. Not 'checkout'.
- HEURISTIC VIOLATED — which principle, by number and name. If none applies, it is an opinion; label it as such.
- OBSERVATION — what is there, stated neutrally and factually. No judgement yet.
- PROBLEM — what breaks and for whom, with the mechanism. 'Users who…, will…, because…'.
- EVIDENCE — screenshot or recording, annotated.
- SEVERITY — 0–4, with the frequency/impact/persistence reasoning stated in one line.
- RECOMMENDATION — a specific change, not a direction. 'Move the shipping cost above the payment step' not 'improve cost transparency'.
- CONFIDENCE — high if it follows from an established principle, lower if it depends on assumptions about your users. Say which.

THE STRUCTURE THAT MAKES FINDINGS LAND:
Observation → Problem → Fix. Separating observation from judgement is what stops a critique from becoming an argument, because the observation is checkable and the room can agree on it before discussing the interpretation.

WHAT TO LEAVE OUT:
- Stacked hedges. 'It might possibly be slightly confusing for some users perhaps' communicates nothing. State the finding and put the uncertainty in the confidence field.
- Solutions disguised as problems. 'The problem is that it needs a tooltip' presumes the fix.
- Aesthetic preference dressed as usability. If you want different type, say you want different type — it is legitimate feedback and it is not a heuristic violation.

REPORT SHAPE: a one-page summary (top five findings with severities and business impact), then the full table, then an appendix of positives. Include the positives — a report that only lists failures is discounted as reflexive criticism.

title: Beyond Nielsen — Other Heuristic Sets Worth Using
content:
SHNEIDERMAN'S EIGHT GOLDEN RULES — closest to Nielsen but sharper on interaction design. Strive for consistency; seek universal usability; offer informative feedback; design dialogues to yield closure; prevent errors; permit easy reversal of actions; keep users in control (internal locus of control); reduce short-term memory load. 'Design dialogues to yield closure' is the one Nielsen lacks and the one most multi-step flows fail — every sequence needs a beginning, middle, and a definite end that tells the user they are finished.

GERHARDT-POWALS' COGNITIVE ENGINEERING PRINCIPLES — best for data-dense and professional interfaces. Automate unwanted workload; reduce uncertainty; fuse data (present derived conclusions, not raw values requiring mental arithmetic); present new information with meaningful aids to interpretation; use names that are conceptually related to function; group data in consequentially meaningful ways; limit data-driven tasks; include only the information the user needs; provide multiple coding of data. 'Fuse data' is the standout for trading dashboards and analytics: if the user must do arithmetic to reach the conclusion, you have offloaded your job.

TOGNAZZINI'S FIRST PRINCIPLES — strongest on anticipation, autonomy, latency reduction, and Fitts's Law. Particularly useful for evaluating perceived performance.

WCAG AS HEURISTICS — Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust. Run these as a fifth heuristic pass; accessibility failures are usability failures with legal weight and are systematically missed by usability-only evaluation.

HEART (Google) — not heuristics but the companion metric frame: Happiness, Engagement, Adoption, Retention, Task success. Use it to convert findings into measurable predictions.

WHEN TO ADD A SET: use Nielsen alone for consumer flows; add Gerhardt-Powals for anything data-heavy; add WCAG always; add domain heuristics for crypto, ecommerce, or AI (he-016).
source: Shneiderman; Gerhardt-Powals (1996); Tognazzini; W3C WCAG; Google HEART

title: AI-Specific Heuristics — Evaluating Probabilistic Interfaces
content:
Nielsen's 10 were written for deterministic software. AI products need the classics adapted plus a set of their own.

THE CLASSICS, ADAPTED:
1. Status — the user knows what the model is doing, what context it is using, and how confident it is.
2. Real world — capabilities framed as user tasks, not model features. No exposed internals.
3. Control — stop generation, undo AI actions, edit outputs, override suggestions. Autonomy always has an exit.
4. Consistency — the same input type produces the same output format; the persona is stable across sessions.
5. Error prevention — guide toward effective prompts; ask a clarifying question rather than producing a bad answer.
6. Recognition — show what the AI can do rather than requiring the user to recall it. The blank box is a recall test.
7. Flexibility — support both guided novice and raw expert modes.
8. Minimalism — outputs are concise and structured. No padding, no unnecessary caveats.
9. Error recovery — failures explained in user terms with a concrete recovery path.
10. Help — teach prompting through the interface, not a docs site.

AI-SPECIFIC HEURISTICS:
- CALIBRATED TRUST — does the interface help the user trust the system the RIGHT amount? Both over-trust (accepting wrong output) and under-trust (verifying everything, so the feature saves nothing) are failures.
- GRACEFUL DEGRADATION — when the model cannot fully help, does it partially help rather than failing completely?
- FEEDBACK EFFECTIVENESS — can the user correct the system easily, and does the correction visibly change anything?
- TRANSPARENCY OF LIMITATIONS — are boundaries clear BEFORE the user hits them, not after?
- APPROPRIATE AUTONOMY — does the system take the right amount of initiative for this task and these stakes?
- CORRECTABILITY OF OUTPUT — is the output in a form the user can edit, or must it be regenerated wholesale?
- ATTRIBUTION — can the user see where a claim came from and check it?

title: Commerce-Specific Heuristics
content:
Run these as an additional pass on any storefront, alongside Nielsen's 10.

- COST TRANSPARENCY — is the full price, including shipping and tax, knowable before the user invests effort? Surprise cost at checkout is the single largest cause of cart abandonment.
- PRODUCT UNDERSTANDING — can the user answer 'is this the right thing for me' without leaving the page? Sizing, materials, dimensions, compatibility, what is in the box.
- AVAILABILITY HONESTY — is stock state accurate, visible before selection, and never a surprise at checkout? Never let a user select an unpurchasable combination.
- TRUST SIGNALS AT THE POINT OF DOUBT — reviews near the buy decision, returns policy near the price, security marks near the payment field, not in the footer.
- FRICTION PROPORTIONALITY — is account creation required before purchase? Guest checkout is the highest-value single fix in most funnels.
- RECOVERY FROM INDECISION — save for later, recently viewed, back-to-results preserving scroll and filters.
- MOBILE PARITY — is every task completable on a phone, one-handed, on a slow connection? Most traffic is mobile; most reviews happen on desktop.
- POST-PURCHASE CONTINUITY — order confirmation, tracking, and returns are part of the product, not an afterthought.
- URGENCY HONESTY — countdown timers that reset, 'only 2 left' that is untrue, and fake social proof are dark patterns with real legal exposure and measurable long-term trust cost.

SHOPIFY SPECIFICS: check that the theme's variant selector reflects availability, that the cart drawer keeps context, that filtering preserves scroll, that the checkout hand-off does not lose visual continuity, and that performance is real — LCP and CLS are conversion factors, so a heuristic pass that ignores speed is incomplete.

title: Crypto and Fintech-Specific Heuristics
content:
- IRREVERSIBILITY LEGIBILITY — before any irreversible action, does the user see the exact consequence in terms they understand: amount, recipient, fee, network, and the fact that it cannot be undone?
- STATE CERTAINTY — is every transaction in a named, visible, explained state (idle / pending / confirming / confirmed / failed), with elapsed and expected time? An unknown state is the category's defining trust failure.
- FEE COMPREHENSION — is the fee shown in fiat as well as native units, before commitment, with an explanation of why it varies?
- ADDRESS SAFETY — is the user ever asked to verify an address by eye? Truncate identically on both sides, highlight matching characters, support ENS/name resolution, and warn on first-time recipients.
- CUSTODY CLARITY — does the user know, at every moment, who controls the assets? Custodial versus self-custodial must never be ambiguous.
- RECOVERY REALITY — does the seed-phrase flow tell the truth about consequences without making the user click through it in a hurry? This is the one place where deliberate, high friction is correct.
- SCAM RESISTANCE — does the interface teach the real terms so users recognise them when attacked? Does it avoid patterns that phishing sites can imitate? Never train users to sign things they cannot read.
- NUMERIC INTEGRITY — no animated numbers, consistent decimal precision, no truncation that changes meaning, explicit currency and unit labels.
- REGULATORY HONESTY — KYC requirements, regional restrictions, and tax implications surfaced before the user invests effort, not after.
- LOSS FRAMING — declines, liquidations, and losses presented factually without either minimising or dramatising.

FINTECH ADDITION: for balances and statements, favour Gerhardt-Powals' 'fuse data' — show the derived conclusion (available to spend, projected shortfall) rather than raw figures the user must combine.

title: Accessibility as a Heuristic Pass
content:
Run this as a distinct pass. Usability evaluation reliably misses accessibility, and accessibility failures carry legal weight.

PERCEIVABLE
- Text contrast: 4.5:1 for body, 3:1 for large text (18.66px bold / 24px regular) and for UI components and graphical objects. Check every state — hover, disabled, placeholder, and error text are where this fails.
- Nothing communicated by colour alone. Error, status, selected, required — all need a second channel.
- All non-decorative images have meaningful alternatives; decorative ones are marked as such.
- Text is real text, not baked into an image.

OPERABLE
- Every interactive element reachable and operable by keyboard, in a logical order.
- Visible focus indicator on everything focusable, with 3:1 contrast against the adjacent background. `outline: none` with no replacement is the most common single failure on the web.
- Touch targets at least 44×44pt (iOS) / 48×48dp (Android), with spacing between them.
- No keyboard traps. Modals trap focus INSIDE deliberately and release it on close, returning focus to the trigger.
- Time limits adjustable or absent; nothing that flashes more than three times per second.

UNDERSTANDABLE
- Labels are persistent, not placeholder-only. Placeholder-as-label fails everyone the moment they type.
- Errors identified in text, adjacent to the field, and programmatically associated with it.
- Consistent navigation and predictable behaviour; nothing changes context on focus.

ROBUST
- Correct semantic roles and names; state changes announced. This cannot be evaluated from a Figma file — specify it in annotations.
- Works at 200% zoom and with text scaling, with no loss of content or function.

DESIGN-STAGE VERDICT: contrast, focus states, target size, label persistence, and non-colour redundancy are ALL decidable from the design file. There is no excuse for finding them after build.

title: Running a Heuristic Evaluation on a Figma File
content:
You do not need a build. Most findings are decidable from the design, and finding them there is an order of magnitude cheaper.

WHAT YOU CAN EVALUATE FROM THE FILE:
- All of heuristic 4 (consistency) — better than in the build, because you can put every button and every error message side by side.
- All of heuristic 8 (minimalism and hierarchy) — squint test on the frames.
- Most of heuristic 2 (language) — read every label.
- Most of heuristic 9 (error messages) — if the error states exist. If they do not, that is finding number one.
- Most of the accessibility pass — contrast, target size, focus states, colour-only signalling, label persistence.
- Heuristic 1 (status) and 5 (error prevention) IF the state inventory exists.

WHAT REQUIRES A PROTOTYPE: heuristic 3 (control and freedom), 6 (recognition across transitions), 7 (efficiency over repeated use), and anything about timing or perceived performance.

METHOD IN FIGMA:
1. Ask for the state inventory first. If only ideal states exist, stop and report that — it is the highest-severity finding available and everything else is premature.
2. Duplicate the file or work on a dedicated 'Review' page so you do not disturb the designer's work.
3. Use FigJam or comments pinned to the exact element. A finding pinned to the element beats a finding in a document.
4. Use Figma's annotation and Dev Mode features to capture accessibility findings where engineering will actually see them.
5. Build a consistency grid: paste every instance of each pattern side by side on one frame. This single artefact finds more real problems than any other technique in this list.
6. Run the theme-toggle test (see figma-prototyping-lore pr-009) — it exposes hardcoded values, dark-mode contrast failures, and token gaps in one pass.
